items.title: Abandoned agent turn leaks its background subprocess (e.g. next build) unbounded → gateway cgroup hits MemoryHigh, event loop starves, all platforms/crons time out

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### Summary

When an agent turn spawns a background tool subprocess (e.g. `pnpm build` / `next build`) and that turn later gets stuck or abandoned, the subprocess is **never reaped and has no lifetime cap**. It keeps running inside the `hermes-gateway` cgroup indefinitely. A single runaway build is enough to push the cgroup past its `MemoryHigh` limit, at which point the kernel throttles and swap-thrashes the gateway process itself — starving its asyncio event loop. The visible result is **every messaging platform disconnecting and every cron failing with "provider timeout, fallback chain exhausted"**, even though the host network and upstream providers are perfectly healthy.

This is a second-order failure: the leaked subprocess doesn't just waste resources, it takes the whole gateway offline via memory-pressure throttling.

### Environment

- hermes-agent `0.18.2`, Linux (Ubuntu 24.04), systemd-managed `hermes-gateway.service`
- Gateway cgroup caps (drop-in): `MemoryHigh=2.4G`, `MemoryMax=4G`, `MemorySwapMax=1G`
- `max_concurrent_children: 2`, `gateway_timeout: 1800`
- Small host (7.6 GB RAM, 4 GB swap)

### Symptoms

- Telegram platform stuck `retrying` — `gateway_state.json`: `"telegram": {"state":"retrying","error_message":"telegram connect timed out after 30s"}` for 3.5+ hours.
- All crons failing: `TimeoutError: Cron job '...' idle for 7872s (limit 600s) — last activity: initializing`, surfaced to the user as *"provider timeout. Fallback chain was exhausted or unavailable."*
- One agent turn logged `response ready: ... time=23829.6s` (6.6 hours for a single response).
- `gateway.log` showing **30+ minute gaps between consecutive lines** for operations nominally bounded by a 30 s timeout, e.g. reconnect attempt 9 started 06:41:48, next line (fallback-IP discovery) at 07:14:36.

### Root cause

Not a network/provider outage — a fresh `curl` to `api.telegram.org` and `api.anthropic.com` from the same host returned in <250 ms throughout.

The actual cause: an agent-run `next build` in a project worktree had been running **~11 hours** at ~90% of a core and ~1.2 GB RSS. Its parent was the gateway PID itself — i.e. a leaked tool subprocess:

```
next build (446753, ~90% CPU, 1.2G, ELAPSED 10:44:00)
  └─ parent: sh -c next build (446752)
       └─ parent: pnpm build (446708)
            └─ parent: hermes gateway (886)   <-- leaked child of the gateway
```

Plus a 24 h-orphaned `typescript-language-server`/`tsserver` (also a gateway child) at ~60% CPU. Together: host load average **21**, RAM exhausted into swap, gateway cgroup `MemoryCurrent` (2.66 G) **over** `MemoryHigh` (2.62 G). Once a cgroup exceeds `MemoryHigh` the kernel applies reclaim throttling + aggressive swap on that cgroup, which stalls the gateway's single asyncio event loop for tens of minutes at a stretch — so every Telegram connect (30 s timeout) and every LLM call times out, and the per-turn/gateway timeouts that *should* fire can't, because the watchdog runs in the same starved loop.

Killing the two leaked trees dropped load 21 → 0.4 instantly, freed ~2.5 GB, and the gateway self-reconnected Telegram within one retry cycle. So the trigger is unambiguously the un-reaped subprocess, not anything network- or provider-side.

### Why existing safeguards didn't catch it

1. **No max lifetime on background tool processes.** They're tracked in `processes.json` and polled by the agent, but nothing bounds their runtime or reaps them when the owning turn ends/aborts. A finite command (`next build`) that hangs runs forever.
2. **The turn timeout doesn't reach descendants.** Even when `gateway_timeout` (1800 s) elapses, the spawned subprocess tree isn't torn down (cf. #71148 for the cron variant of "timeout kill doesn't reach descendants").
3. **The turn-timeout watchdog itself is starved.** Because it shares the throttled event loop, it can't fire while the cgroup is thrashing — so the stuck turn ran 6.6 h.

### Suggested fixes

- Enforce a **maximum lifetime** (and/or idle cap) on background tool subprocesses, killing the whole process tree (`killpg` / cgroup kill) on expiry.
- On turn completion **or abort/timeout**, tear down subprocesses that turn spawned — reap descendants, not just the direct child.
- Consider running each agent turn's tool subprocesses in a **dedicated child cgroup** with its own memory cap, so a runaway build can't induce `MemoryHigh` pressure on the gateway's own cgroup and take the event loop down with it.
- Optionally: make the per-turn watchdog resilient to event-loop starvation (e.g. a separate thread/process or a hard `MemoryMax` on the tool cgroup so the kernel OOM-kills the runaway before it starves the gateway).

### Related

- #71148 — cron timeout leaves orphaned process trees (same "timeout doesn't reach descendants" mechanism, cron path)
- #37454 (closed) — orphan processes in cgroup blocking systemd restart
- #48339 — background process tracker shows stale "running" status

items.title: Desktop updater infinite retry loop: no backoff on exit 2 causes deadlock with stale update marker

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Problem

The Desktop built-in updater (`hermes-setup --update`) enters an infinite retry loop when `hermes update` exits with code 2 (concurrent update guard). Each retry spawns a new Tauri updater process within ~1.5 seconds, but the venv is still locked by the previous attempt, causing every retry to fail with the same error.

## Root Cause

The Desktop Electron app spawns the Tauri updater as a detached process. When the updater fails with exit code 2, the Desktop immediately re-spawns a new updater — **no backoff, no max retry limit**. Each new updater:

1. Acquires the update marker (`~/.hermes/.hermes-update-in-progress`) with its own PID
2. Spawns `hermes update` as a child
3. `hermes update` hits the venv lock from the previous attempt → exits with code 2
4. Tauri updater surfaces the error and exits
5. Desktop detects failure → immediately spawns a new updater → goto 1

This creates an infinite loop lasting up to 20 minutes (the `UPDATE_MARKER_MAX_AGE_SECS` ceiling).

## Evidence

From `~/.hermes/logs/bootstrap-installer.log`:

```
2026-07-31T01:42:31.380Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib: Hermes installer starting mode=Update
2026-07-31T01:42:32.000Z  ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 20545, started 0s ago).
2026-07-31T01:42:33.616Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib: Hermes installer starting mode=Update
2026-07-31T01:42:33.746Z  ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 20545, started 2s ago).
2026-07-31T01:42:35.332Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib: Hermes installer starting mode=Update
2026-07-31T01:42:35.466Z  ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 20545, started 4s ago).
...repeats every ~1.5s for 20 minutes...
```

Each "Hermes installer starting" is a **new process** (different parent PID each time), all hitting the same stale marker from the first failed attempt.

## Suggested Fix

1. Add exponential backoff to the Desktop's update retry logic (e.g., 5s → 10s → 20s → give up after 3 attempts)
2. Cap max retries at 3, then surface a persistent error message to the user
3. Clean stale markers before spawning a new updater (the marker PID is from a previous updater that already exited)
4. Alternatively, the Tauri updater could clean the marker on exit even on failure paths

## Workaround

```bash
pkill -f "hermes-setup.*--update" 2>/dev/null
rm -f ~/.hermes/.hermes-update-in-progress
hermes update
```

## Environment

- macOS darwin-arm64
- Hermes Agent v0.19.1
- Electron 40.10.2
- cua-driver 0.14.2

items.title: [Bug]: validate_deferred_call_args in tool_search.py rejects deferred MCP tools when invoked via tool_call

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

When calling deferred MCP tools via `tool_call` (e.g. `mcp__chrome_remote_win__new_page` or `mcp__codebase_memory_mcp__get_architecture`), the probe validation function `validate_deferred_call_args` in `tools/tool_search.py` misvalidates the arguments passed by the model and rejects valid tool executions with errors such as:

```json
{
  "error": "tool_call to 'mcp__chrome_remote_win__new_page' is missing required argument(s): url. The tool was NOT invoked.",
  "parameters": { ... },
  "hint": "Retry tool_call with 'arguments' matching the parameters schema above."
}
```

Even when the model provides the exact required arguments inside `tool_call(name=..., arguments={...})`, the call is aborted before invocation.

## Root Cause Analysis

In `tools/tool_search.py`, `validate_deferred_call_args(name, args)` validates `args` against the tool's `required` parameter schema:

```python
missing = [r for r in required if isinstance(r, str) and r not in args]
```

When `validate_deferred_call_args` is invoked from `agent/tool_executor.py` or `model_tools.py`, if `args` is passed as the outer `tool_call` parameters object (or an unparsed/empty arguments dict) rather than the unwrapped underlying tool arguments, `r not in args` evaluates to `True` for every required field. As a result, the probe validator assumes required arguments are missing and intercepts the call, returning a schema hint error rather than allowing the call to dispatch to the MCP server.

## Environment Details

- **Hermes Version**: Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30) · upstream `15cb86eb`
- **OS / Environment**: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS under WSL2 (Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64)
- **Python**: 3.11.15
- **Affected Subsystem**: `tools/tool_search.py` (`validate_deferred_call_args`), `agent/tool_executor.py`, `model_tools.py`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an MCP server with tools that have `required` fields (e.g., `chrome-devtools-mcp` with `new_page` requiring `url`, or `codebase-memory-mcp` with `get_architecture` requiring `project`).
2. Invoke the tool via `tool_call`:
   ```json
   {
     "name": "tool_call",
     "arguments": {
       "name": "mcp__chrome_remote_win__new_page",
       "arguments": {
         "url": "https://example.com"
       }
     }
   }
   ```
3. `validate_deferred_call_args` is triggered during probe validation and returns a `missing required argument(s)` error response without executing the tool.

## Proposed Fix

Ensure that `validate_deferred_call_args` receives the unwrapped `underlying_args` dictionary (parsed from `arguments`), or adjust `validate_deferred_call_args` to safely unwrap nested `arguments` if passed directly.

items.title: [Bug]: terminal/execute_code env ignores the multiplexer's secret scope — routed profiles get the default profile's credentials

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

items.body:
### Bug Description

Under `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true`, `_profile_runtime_scope` (`gateway/run.py`) correctly installs the routed profile's credentials via `set_secret_scope(build_profile_secret_scope(...))`, and its docstring states the invariant:

> so `get_secret` reads this profile's keys and never the process-global `os.environ` (which in a multiplexer may hold another profile's values)

But the **terminal** and **execute_code** environments never consult that scope. `tools/environments/local.py::_make_run_env` builds from the process environment:

```python
merged = dict(os.environ | env)
```

and the Docker backend's `_docker_env_args` (`tools/environments/docker.py`) resolves each forwarded key with `value = os.getenv(key)`.

Neither module imports `agent.secret_scope` or calls `get_secret()`. Since the gateway process starts under the **default** profile, `os.environ` holds the default profile's `.env`. So under multiplexing, **every routed profile's shell receives the default profile's credentials**, regardless of what its own `.env` says.

This is distinct from #61046 (profile `.env` not loaded at startup) and #75141 (startup does not unset inherited keys). Those produce a *missing or stale* value — the tool fails with a 401 and you find out. This one produces a *valid credential belonging to a different profile*: the call succeeds, the data comes back, and nothing logs anything. It fails **open**.

The docs are accurate about the current scope — the multi-profile-gateways page says *"subprocesses like MCP servers and Kanban workers only ever see their own profile's secrets"*, naming MCP and Kanban and not the terminal. The gap is that any credential consumed by a CLI the agent runs (rather than by Hermes itself) falls outside that guarantee, and nothing warns you.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Two profiles, `A` (default) and `B`.
2. `~/.hermes/.env` (profile A): `SERVICE_TOKEN=token_for_A`
3. `~/.hermes/profiles/B/.env`: `SERVICE_TOKEN=token_for_B`
4. Add `SERVICE_TOKEN` to `terminal.env_passthrough` in both profiles.
5. `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true`, with a `gateway.profile_routes` entry routing some channel to profile `B`.
6. From that channel, have the agent run a shell command that echoes `$SERVICE_TOKEN` (or run any CLI that authenticates with it).

### Expected Behavior

The turn is routed to profile `B`, so its shell should see `token_for_B` — matching what `get_secret("SERVICE_TOKEN")` returns inside the same turn.

### Actual Behavior

The shell sees `token_for_A`. `get_secret()` and the terminal disagree within a single turn: the scoped path returns B's value, the subprocess path returns A's.

### Impact

Where profiles exist to give agents *different levels of access* (rather than only different personas), this silently collapses them onto the default profile's authority. If the default profile is the broadest — a reasonable and common setup, since it is usually the original one — every narrower profile is silently promoted to it. Because the credential is valid, there is no error, no log line, and no observable difference from correct behaviour.

### Suggested Fix

Resolve passthrough keys through `agent.secret_scope.get_secret()` when a scope is active, falling back to `os.environ` when it is not, in both:

- `tools/environments/local.py::_make_run_env`
- `tools/environments/docker.py::_docker_env_args`

`get_secret` already has the right semantics for this: it falls back transparently when multiplexing is off, so single-profile gateways are unaffected, and it fails closed on an unscoped read when multiplexing is on.

Worth considering alongside #59286, which is the same class for the Daytona backend — allowlisted env not reaching the sandbox. There may be value in one shared helper that every backend uses to resolve a passthrough key, so a new backend cannot reintroduce this by construction.

### Related

- #61046 — profile `.env` not loaded (missing value; fails closed)
- #75141 — startup does not unset inherited keys (stale value; fails closed)
- #59286 — Daytona backend ignores `terminal.env_passthrough`
- #69820 — `execute_code` inherits another request's session ID via env passthrough

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop file explorer pane doesn't follow active session cwd when opening an existing session (stays on home dir)

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Bug Description

When opening an **existing** session whose workspace is a project directory (e.g. `H:/obsidian-vault/印尼日记`), the file explorer pane (bottom-right, "FUTSIANG" tab) stays on the remembered home directory (`C:/Users/futsiang`), showing dotfolders (.aws, .cursor, .ssh, ...) instead of the session's working directory. The session itself is correctly grouped under its Project in the sidebar, and the embedded terminal does follow the session cwd — only the file explorer pane is out of sync.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a session created under a named Project (e.g. 印尼日记, cwd `H:/obsidian-vault/印尼日记`) — created via the Project row's `+` button.
2. Quit the app / open a different project's session so the remembered workspace cwd becomes home or another dir.
3. Click the existing 印尼日记 session in the sidebar to reopen it.
4. Observe: sidebar shows the session under 印尼日记 ✅, terminal starts at the session dir ✅, but the **file explorer pane still lists `C:/Users/futsiang`** (home) ❌.

Reproduced with sessions `20260724_131226_72534a` and `20260722_104403_186f0d` — both have correct `cwd`/git_repo_root in state.db but the explorer pane does not follow. Note: *some* sessions DO follow correctly, so behavior is inconsistent.

## Expected Behavior

Opening an existing session should sync the file explorer pane to that session's cwd (same as the terminal).

## Actual Behavior

The file explorer pane keeps showing the last remembered workspace cwd (home), independent of which session is active.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- App: Hermes Desktop (chat surface)
- Model: deepseek-v4-flash
- Source: git install at D:/hermes (main)

## Source-level observation (may help triage)

- `apps/desktop/src/app/session/workspace-session-target.ts` — `startWorkspaceSession` calls `setCurrentCwd(target)` only for **new** sessions; reopening an existing session does not go through this path, so cwd is not synced.
- `apps/desktop/src/store/session.ts:448` — `$currentCwd = atom(getRememberedWorkspaceCwd())` seeds from localStorage `hermes.desktop.workspace-cwd`, which persists across sessions.
- `seedLiveCwd()` (session.ts:141-143) only sets cwd when `!$activeSessionId.get()` — i.e. no active session yet; reopening a stored session leaves the pane on the remembered value.
- Inconsistency (some sessions follow, some don't) may relate to `followActiveSessionCwd` (store/projects.ts:293) refreshing the view only in the `explicitTarget` branch of `startWorkspaceSession`.

items.title: [Bug]: hermes chat --provider moa without -m <preset> KeyErrors on agent.model, then silently falls back with no MoA

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Bug Description

`hermes chat --provider moa` without `-m <preset>` leaves `agent.model` holding the user's primary model name (e.g. `kimi-k3`). The MoA client builders pass that value straight through as the preset selector, and `resolve_moa_preset()` raises `KeyError` because it is not a preset key. After 3 retries the turn silently falls back to a fallback provider (e.g. `deepseek-v4-flash`), which answers with no MoA involvement — the command appears to succeed while the requested mixture never runs.

## Reproduction

```bash
# config.yaml: model.default = kimi-k3 (any non-preset primary model name)
hermes chat -q "What is 17 times 23? Reply with just the number." --provider moa
```

Works correctly (all slots fire) only when the preset name is passed explicitly:

```bash
hermes chat -q "..." --provider moa -m default
```

## Expected vs Actual

**Expected:** `--provider moa` selects MoA with the configured `default_preset` when `-m` is absent or names a non-preset model — matching how the in-session switcher resolves bare `moa` via `default_preset` (see #71244 for the adjacent `-m moa` inconsistency).

**Actual:** three `KeyError: '<model name>'` retries, then silent fallback to a non-MoA provider. Correct-looking answer, wrong pipeline.

## Log evidence

```
INFO  agent.turn_context: conversation turn: session=... model=kimi-k3 provider=moa platform=cli msg='What is 17 times 23?...'
WARN  agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 1/3) error_type=KeyError provider=moa base_url=moa://local model=kimi-k3 summary='kimi-k3'
WARN  agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 2/3) error_type=KeyError provider=moa ... summary='kimi-k3'
WARN  agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 3/3) error_type=KeyError provider=moa ... summary='kimi-k3'
INFO  agent.chat_completion_helpers: Fallback activated: kimi-k3 → deepseek-v4-flash (deepseek)
```

## Root cause

`resolve_moa_preset(config, name)` (`hermes_cli/moa_config.py`) raises `KeyError(name)` for any name that is not a preset key. That strictness is correct for explicit preset selection — but three call sites feed it `agent.model`, which on the MoA virtual provider is a *model* name, not a preset name:

1. `agent/agent_init.py` — `elif agent.provider == "moa":` → `MoAClient(agent.model or "default")`. Startup path for `--provider moa`. The `KeyError` surfaces on the first API call inside `MoAChatCompletions.create()` (`agent/moa_loop.py`, `resolve_moa_preset(load_config().get("moa") or {}, self.preset_name)`).
2. `agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py` — the `switch_model` MoA branch does the same `MoAClient(agent.model or "default")` for provider-only switches.
3. `agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py` — `anthropic_prompt_cache_policy` MoA branch calls `resolve_moa_preset(cfg, eff_model or None)` inside a broad `except Exception`, so the same mismatch silently returns `(False, False)` and the MoA aggregator loses prompt caching even when the turn itself works.

In-session paths (`/moa <prompt>`, `/model <preset> --provider moa`) are unaffected: they resolve `default_preset` / exact preset names before construction.

## Suggested fix

Keep `resolve_moa_preset` strict; add a lenient selector for the `agent.model` inheritance boundary, and use it at all three sites:

```python
def resolve_moa_preset_name(config, name=None) -> str:
    """Return ``name`` when it is a configured preset, else the default preset."""
    cfg = normalize_moa_config(config)
    clean = str(name or "").strip()
    if clean and clean in cfg["presets"]:
        return clean
    return str(cfg.get("default_preset") or DEFAULT_MOA_PRESET_NAME)
```

I have this implemented locally with regression tests (`tests/hermes_cli/test_moa_config.py`: known preset honored, model name / None / "" → default, strict `resolve_moa_preset` still raises) and verified live: the repro command above now fans out to all reference models plus the aggregator (14.9s, correct answer, no KeyError). Happy to contribute it as a PR if the approach looks right.

## Related

- #71244 — MoA selection inconsistencies (`-m moa` bare, `/model moa --global`); same theme, different selection path
- #65875 — desktop "new sessions hang silently with MoA KeyError" (same exception family, different entry point)

Summary
Add a visual progress bar at the bottom of the chat interface showing current context usage vs. maximum context window.

## Problem
Currently, users cannot visually gauge how much of their context window is being used. This makes it difficult to:
- Know when context compression is triggered
- Understand if we're approaching the context limit
- Debug "Cannot compress further" errors

## Proposed Solution
Add a progress bar component to the UI with:
- **Visual indicator**: Horizontal bar showing usage percentage
- **Tooltip/label**: Display "Current: X tokens / Max: Y tokens (Z%)"
- **Color coding**: 
  - Green: <50% usage
  - Yellow: 50-80% usage  
  - Red: >80% usage (warning)
- **Location**: Bottom of chat interface, near status bar

## Implementation Notes
- Read context usage from `context_engine.get_context_stats()` or similar
- Max context from `model_metadata.MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH`
- Update in real-time as messages are added/removed

## Reference
User reported this was available in a previous version, suggesting it may have been removed or never fully implemented.

## Priority
Medium - Improves UX and debugging experience

items.title: [Feature]: Roadmap Proposal: Multi-Session Collaboration for Hermes Agent

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

# Roadmap Proposal: Multi-Session Collaboration for Hermes Agent

> **Author**: Community contributor
> **Context**: Multi-LLM session collaboration (e.g., Strategist/Executor pattern)
> **Repository**: Hermes Agent (NousResearch)
> **Date**: 2026-08-01

---

## 1. Problem Statement

When orchestrating multiple LLM sessions in a structured collaboration loop
(e.g., **S**trategist → **A**ctor), users hit a fundamental gap: **sessions are
isolated islands**. There is no native way for two sessions to:

1. Share a persistent, isolated context (each session keeps its own memory across
   turns, independent of the other)
2. Send messages to each other (one session can't prompt another)
3. Share state information (task status, file changes, findings)
4. Run simultaneously and communicate actively (not just the parent
   delegating to a child)

This forces users into brittle workarounds: manual tmux orchestration, file
queues, or re-reading the entire project context on every `delegate_task` call.

---

## 2. Current Gaps

| Capability | Today | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| `delegate_task` — persistent session | ❌ Each call is a fresh session, no memory | Context must be manually rebuilt each turn |
| `delegate_task` — profile/memory isolation | ❌ No `profile` parameter | S and A share the same memory; no isolation |
| `prompt.submit` — cross-session | ❌ Binds to connected transport | Can't send a message to another session |
| `prompt.background` — persistent | ❌ `skip_memory=True`, temp session_id | Same problem as `delegate_task` |
| Session pairing / handshake | ❌ Does not exist | No way for sessions to know about each other |
| Shared state layer | ❌ Does not exist | Sessions can't share task status or findings |

---


### Proposed Solution


## 3. Three Implementation Paths

The proposal is structured as three progressive paths. Each one is
**self-contained** — Hermes can adopt any subset. Paths B and C depend on
infrastructure introduced in earlier paths.

### Path A — `delegate_task` with `profile` parameter
**Scope**: Make delegated subagents persistent and isolated.
**Estimated effort**: 1–2 days, 3 files changed.

---

#### What changes

**File 1: `tools/delegate_tool.py` — Add `profile` parameter**

```python
DELEGATE_TASK_SCHEMA["parameters"]["properties"]["profile"] = {
    "type": "string",
    "description": (
        "Persistent profile name. Subagent loads this profile's memory "
        "directory and session history, giving it durable context across turns. "
        "Profiles are isolated — A's memory is never visible to B."
    ),
    "examples": ["A", "B"],
}
```

**File 2: `run_agent.py` — Load profile memory into system prompt**

```python
class AIAgent:
    def __init__(self, ..., profile: str = None):
        self._profile = profile
        if profile:
            self._memory_file = Path.home() / ".hermes" / "profiles" / profile / "memory.md"
            # Inject into system prompt on every turn (same mechanism as Pi)
            self._profile_memory = self._memory_file.read_text() if self._memory_file.exists() else ""
```

**File 3: `run_agent.py` — Session history lookup when `profile` is set**

```python
def _resolve_session_for_profile(self, profile: str) -> str | None:
    """Return the most recent session_id for the given profile, or None."""
    ...  # Query state.db by profile tag
```

When `profile` is set and `_profile_memory` exists, the memory file is injected
into the system prompt on every API call, and session history (if available) is
loaded into `conversation_history`. When `profile` is not set, behaviour is
**identical to today** — backward compatible.

---

#### Usage

```python
# S (strategist) discovers a bug
delegate_task(
    profile="A",
    goal="Verify the log_path=NULL bug in execution_worker.py line 91",
    context="Bug: _check_stale_before_pickup() skips recovery when log_path=NULL",
    role="leaf",
)
# A reads its own memory.md, remembers prior findings, verifies and returns

# S reviews, forms a decision
delegate_task(
    profile="A",
    goal="Apply the fix",
    context="Decision: add log_path fallback using task_id to infer log path",
    role="leaf",
)
# A still has memory of the prior verification, executes the fix
```

---

#### Memory layout

```
~/.hermes/profiles/
├── S/
│   └── memory.md     ← S's judgment history, design decisions
└── A/
    └── memory.md     ← A's verification results, execution records
```

**Benefits**: ✅ Persistent memory, ✅ Isolation, ✅ Different models per profile,
✅ Minimal change, ✅ Backward compatible.
**Limitations**: ❌ No cross-session messaging (still parent-child pattern).

---

### Path B — `session.send` RPC (Cross-Session Messaging)
**Scope**: Any session can send a message to any other session and receive a reply.
**Estimated effort**: 3–5 days, 2 new RPC methods + 1 helper.

---

#### What changes

**New file: `tui_gateway/methods_session.py` — add three methods**

```python
@method("session.send")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Send a message to a target session and receive a reply.

    Implementation:
    1. Resolve the target session from its session_id
    2. Load the target's full history and memory.md
    3. Spawn an AIAgent instance for that session
    4. Run one turn of conversation with the incoming text
    5. Append the exchange to the target session's history in state.db
    6. Return synchronously (wait=True) or emit session.complete (wait=False)
    """
    target_id = params["target"]       # session_id of the target
    text = params["text"]
    wait = params.get("wait", True)

    if not _session_exists(target_id):
        return _err(rid, 4040, f"session not found: {target_id}")

    history = _load_session_history(target_id)
    memory = _load_session_memory(target_id)

    result = AIAgent(
        conversation_history=history,
        ephemeral_system_prompt=memory,
        quiet_mode=True,
        verbose_logging=False,
        session_id=target_id,
        max_iterations=30,
    ).chat(text)

    _append_session_message(target_id, "user", text)
    _append_session_message(target_id, "assistant", result)

    if wait:
        return _ok(rid, {"result": result, "session_id": target_id})
    else:
        _emit("session.complete", rid, {
            "session_id": target_id,
            "task_id": params.get("task_id", ""),
            "result": result,
        })
        return _ok(rid, {"queued": True})


@method("session.query")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Query the last N messages from a target session."""
    target_id = params["target"]
    last = params.get("last", 1)
    messages = _get_last_messages(target_id, last=last)
    return _ok(rid, {"messages": messages, "session_id": target_id})


@method("session.create_role")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Create a persistent role session with persona and memory.

    Creates a session in state.db, writes memory.md to the session's directory,
    and optionally configures a default model.
    """
    name = params["name"]              # e.g. "A", "B"
    memory = params["memory"]          # initial memory.md content
    persona = params.get("persona", "")  # system prompt addition
    model = params.get("model")         # override default
    provider = params.get("provider")

    session_id = _create_session_in_db(name=name)
    _write_session_memory(session_id, memory)
    if persona:
        _set_session_persona(session_id, persona)
    if model or provider:
        _set_session_model(session_id, model, provider)

    return _ok(rid, {
        "session_id": session_id,
        "name": name,
        "status": "created",
    })
```

**Helper: `tui_gateway/server.py` — cross-transport session spawn**

The key implementation detail is that `session.send` does **not** require the
target session to have an active transport connection. It spawns a one-shot
`AIAgent` that loads the target's history and memory, runs one turn, and
persists the result. This is structurally similar to `prompt.background`
but with two critical differences: it loads the target's real history (not
`skip_memory=True`) and writes the exchange back to the target session's
history so subsequent calls accumulate context.

---

#### S/A Collaboration Loop

```
# Initialization
session.create_role(
    name="A",
    model="claude-sonnet-4",
    memory="你是执行者A。项目路径: .../reddit-monitor/",
    persona="你只负责验证和修改代码，不要做架构决策"
)
→ {session_id: "A-session-xxx"}

# Step 1: S verifies bug
session.send(
    target="A-session-xxx",
    text="发现bug: execution_worker.py line 91，log_path=NULL 时跳过恢复逻辑"
)
→ {result: "已确认。log_path=NULL 时 fallback 到 task_id 推断路径", ...}

session.query(target="A-session-xxx", last=3)
→ [S的bug描述, A的确认回复]

# Step 2: S decides, A executes
session.send(
    target="A-session-xxx",
    text="S的决策: 修改 line 91，添加 log_path=NULL 时的 fallback 逻辑"
)
→ {result: "已修改。commit: 3228074", ...}

# S 自己验证，完成后结束
```

Each call to `session.send` accumulates into A's session history. A always
sees the full conversation. S doesn't need to rebuild context.

---

#### Implementation detail: `wait=False` + event-based

For long-running tasks (e.g., crawl_sources taking 20+ minutes), the `wait`

@method("session.pair")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Register a session as a collaborator of the calling session.

    Both sessions receive an event and load each other's shared state.
    """
    s_id = params["session_id"]
    partner_id = params["partner"]
    name = params.get("name", partner_id[:12])
    model = params.get("model")
    _register_pair(s_id, partner_id, name, model)
    _emit("session.paired", partner_id, {
        "partner": s_id,
        "name": name,
        "model": model,
    })
    # Both sessions reload shared state into their context
    _rebuild_injection(s_id)
    _rebuild_injection(partner_id)
    return _ok(rid, {"paired": True, "partner_session": partner_id})


@method("session.list_partners")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """List partners of the calling session."""
    sid = params["session_id"]
    partners = _get_partners(sid)
    return _ok(rid, {
        "partners": [
            {"session_id": p["id"], "name": p["name"],
             "model": p.get("model", ""),
             "last_shared_at": p.get("last_shared_at", "")}
            for p in partners
        ]
    })


@method("session.init_context")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Rebuild a session's injected context after a pairing change."""
    sid = params["session_id"]
    injection = _build_shared_injection(sid)
    return _ok(rid, {"injection": injection})
```

**Session initialization injection**

When a session starts (or is activated), the framework automatically injects
a shared state header into the system prompt:

```

  task.file = "execution_worker.py:91"

This is built fresh on each turn (not cached), so the context is always

## 5. Design Decisions for Hermes Team to Consider

These are open questions that affect implementation but don't change the
proposed API surface:

1. **Memory injection timing**: Should memory.md be re-read every turn
   (like Pi), or read once at session start? Every-turn is more accurate
   but costs tokens per turn. The proposal assumes every-turn for consistency
   with existing memory behaviour, but Hermes may prefer read-once for cost.

2. **Transport model for `session.send`**: The proposal assumes a
   one-shot agent spawn without an active transport. An alternative is to
   route through a long-lived worker pool (like `prompt.background` uses)
   for concurrent message handling.

3. **Shared state storage**: File-based JSON is simplest and works across
   processes. For high-frequency updates, SQLite would be more performant.

4. **`wait=False` timeout**: When `session.send(wait=False)` is used, how
   long should the server wait for the background task before emitting
   `session.complete`? A default of 30 minutes with a configurable
   `timeout_minutes` parameter is suggested.

5. **Pairing security**: Should pairing require explicit confirmation from
   both sessions (two-way handshake), or is unilateral registration
   sufficient? The proposal assumes unilateral but notes the option.

6. **Multi-model coordination**: When S uses model A and A uses model B,
   should Hermes enforce that A's responses are in the same language/format
   as S's? The proposal assumes no enforcement — both sessions are free to
   use whatever model they have configured.

### Path B — `session.send` RPC (Cross-Session Messaging)
**Scope**: Any session can send a message to any other session and receive a reply.
**Estimated effort**: 3–5 days, 2 new RPC methods + 1 helper.

#### What changes

**New file: `tui_gateway/methods_session.py` — add three methods**

```python
@method("session.send")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Send a message to a target session and receive a reply.

    Implementation:
    1. Resolve the target session from its session_id
    2. Load the target's full history and memory.md
    3. Spawn an AIAgent instance for that session
    4. Run one turn of conversation with the incoming text
    5. Append the exchange to the target session's history in state.db
    6. Return synchronously (wait=True) or emit session.complete (wait=False)
    """
    target_id = params["target"]       # session_id of the target
    text = params["text"]
    wait = params.get("wait", True)

    if not _session_exists(target_id):
        return _err(rid, 4040, f"session not found: {target_id}")

    history = _load_session_history(target_id)
    memory = _load_session_memory(target_id)

    result = AIAgent(
        conversation_history=history,
        ephemeral_system_prompt=memory,
        quiet_mode=True,
        verbose_logging=False,
        session_id=target_id,
        max_iterations=30,
    ).chat(text)

    _append_session_message(target_id, "user", text)
    _append_session_message(target_id, "assistant", result)

    if wait:
        return _ok(rid, {"result": result, "session_id": target_id})
    else:
        _emit("session.complete", rid, {
            "session_id": target_id,
            "task_id": params.get("task_id", ""),
            "result": result,
        })
        return _ok(rid, {"queued": True})


@method("session.query")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Query the last N messages from a target session."""
    target_id = params["target"]
    last = params.get("last", 1)
    messages = _get_last_messages(target_id, last=last)
    return _ok(rid, {"messages": messages, "session_id": target_id})


@method("session.create_role")
def _(rid, params: dict) -> dict:
    """Create a persistent role session with persona and memory.

    Creates a session in state.db, writes memory.md to the session's directory,
    and optionally configures a default model.
    """
    name = params["name"]              # e.g. "A", "B"
    memory = params["memory"]          # initial memory.md content
    persona = params.get("persona", "")  # system prompt addition
    model = params.get("model")         # override default
    provider = params.get("provider")

    session_id = _create_session_in_db(name=name)
    _write_session_memory(session_id, memory)
    if persona:
        _set_session_persona(session_id, persona)
    if model or provider:
        _set_session_model(session_id, model, provider)

    return _ok(rid, {
        "session_id": session_id,
        "name": name,
        "status": "created",
    })
```

**Helper: `tui_gateway/server.py` — cross-transport session spawn**

The key implementation detail is that `session.send` does **not** require the
target session to have an active transport connection. It spawns a one-shot
`AIAgent` that loads the target's history and memory, runs one turn, and
persists the result. This is structurally similar to `prompt.background`
but with two critical differences: it loads the target's real history (not
`skip_memory=True`) and writes the exchange back to the target session's
history so subsequent calls accumulate context.

These are open questions that affect implementation but don't change the
proposed API surface:

1. **Memory injection timing**: Should memory.md be re-read every turn
   (like Pi), or read once at session start? Every-turn is more accurate
   but costs tokens per turn. The proposal assumes every-turn for consistency
   with existing memory behaviour, but Hermes may prefer read-once for cost.

2. **Transport model for `session.send`**: The proposal assumes a
   one-shot agent spawn without an active transport. An alternative is to
   route through a long-lived worker pool (like `prompt.background` uses)
   for concurrent message handling.

3. **Shared state storage**: File-based JSON is simplest and works across
   processes. For high-frequency updates, SQLite would be more performant.

4. **`wait=False` timeout**: When `session.send(wait=False)` is used, how
   long should the server wait for the background task before emitting
   `session.complete`? A default of 30 minutes with a configurable
   `timeout_minutes` parameter is suggested.

5. **Pairing security**: Should pairing require explicit confirmation from
   both sessions (two-way handshake), or is unilateral registration
   sufficient? The proposal assumes unilateral but notes the option.

6. **Multi-model coordination**: When S uses model A and A uses model B,
   should Hermes enforce that A's responses are in the same language/format
   as S's? The proposal assumes no enforcement — both sessions are free to
   use whatever model they have configured.

---

## 6. Related Work

| Project | Approach | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| **Pi Agent** (`earendil-works/pi`) | Independent processes, memory.md injected per turn | File-based persistent memory works for multi-agent |
| **Pi chat** (`earendil-works/pi-chat`) | Per-channel memory + shared storage + skills | Persistent memory + skills across channels |
| **Hermes Kanban** | SQLite board, dispatcher, worker isolation | Task queuing and worker isolation at infra level |
| **Hermes Profiles** | Per-profile config, memory, sessions | Isolation infrastructure already exists |
| **Claude Code** | Single session, no cross-session messaging | Single-session model limits collaboration |
| **Codex** | Single session, no cross-session messaging | Same limitation |

The key insight: **Hermes already has the pieces** (profiles, sessions,
memory, state.db). They just aren't connected through the delegation and
messaging layers. This proposal connects them.

---

## 7. Summary Table

| | A: `profile` on `delegate_task` | B: `session.send` RPC | C: Pairing + Shared State |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Persistent memory** | ✅ Profile memory | ✅ Session history | ✅ Both |
| **Context isolation** | ✅ Per profile | ✅ Per session | ✅ Per session + shared layer |
| **Cross-session messaging** | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Bidirectional** | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Shared state** | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| **Different models** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Estimated effort** | 1–2 days | 3–5 days | 1–2 weeks |
| **New modules** | None | None | 1 (`shared_state.py`) |
| **New tool types** | None | None | 1 (`shared_state`) |
| **New RPC methods** | None | 3 | 3 |
| **Backward compatible** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **File count changed** | 3 | 2 | 4–5 |

---

## 8. Suggested Hermes Team Actions

1. **Evaluate Path A** — smallest change, highest immediate value for
   `delegate_task` users. Low risk, no new surface area.
2. **Evaluate Path B** — enables session-to-session messaging. This is the
   most architecturally "clean" approach (uses existing session model).
3. **Defer Path C** — implement only if Path A + B are adopted and users
   demonstrate demand for full peer-to-peer collaboration. The shared state
   store can be designed to be additive without breaking Phases 1–2.

---

*This proposal is structured so Hermes can adopt any subset independently.*
*The paths are ordered by dependency and effort. Hermes's team should
evaluate based on their roadmap priorities, not this ordering.*

items.title: Hermes Desktop: backend not reliably drained/killed on app quit (stray hermes serve orphans)
items.body:
## Bug

Hermes Desktop's \`before-quit\` handler calls \`stopBackendChild()\` / \`stopAllPoolBackends()\` but doesn't wait for the SIGTERM to actually take effect before letting Electron proceed with quit. If the backend needs longer than expected to exit, the child is orphaned instead of exiting cleanly.

## Fix

In \`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts\`'s \`before-quit\` handler:
- Capture the primary + pooled backend child processes *before* calling \`stopAllPoolBackends()\` (it deletes pool map entries before killing, so reading the pool after yields nothing).
- \`event.preventDefault()\`, hide windows immediately (Cmd-Q should feel instant even though we're delaying the actual process exit), then \`Promise.allSettled\` a bounded wait (5s) for every still-alive child to exit before calling \`app.quit()\`.
- Guard with a one-shot latch so the \`app.quit()\` this schedules doesn't re-enter \`before-quit\` and reschedule the same drain.

Companion to timeout_graceful_shutdown on the Python side (see the uvicorn shutdown-hang issue) — that fix bounds *how long* a backend can take to exit; this fix makes the desktop actually *wait* for it instead of racing ahead.

Verified: 912/912 existing Electron tests pass with this change; manual quit test showed only the gateway process surviving (correct) with no stray \`hermes serve\`.

items.title: browser_tool.py: orphaned Chromium daemons accumulate for weeks despite reaper thread (owner_pid check likely too coarse)
items.body:
## Summary

`browser_tool.py` has a background reaper (`_reap_orphaned_browser_sessions`, called periodically by `_browser_cleanup_thread_worker` and also on `atexit`) that is supposed to kill orphaned `agent-browser` daemons and their Chromium process trees when the owning hermes process has died. In practice, on a long-running gateway instance, orphaned Chromium processes accumulated for **up to 16 days** and were never reaped.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.16.0 (2026.6.5), running as `gateway run` inside an LXC container (Ubuntu 24.04, Proxmox)
- Long-lived gateway process, single PID, running continuously since initial start (19+ days uptime at time of investigation), never restarted or crashed
- `browser.inactivity_timeout: 120` (default) in config.yaml

## Evidence

Found on 2026-08-01 via `ps aux | grep chromium`:

- **117 chromium processes** running, spanning **13 distinct orphaned sessions** (distinguishable by unique `--user-data-dir=/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX` and `--remote-debugging-port=NNNNN` per session)
- Session start dates: Jul 16, Jul 17, Jul 25, Jul 26 (x2), Jul 27, Jul 29 (x2), Jul 30 (x2), Jul 31 (x2) — i.e. orphans from **16 different days**, continuously accumulating rather than being cleaned up
- Each orphaned session was a full Chromium process tree: main browser process, 2x crashpad_handler, gpu-process, 2x utility (network/storage), 3x renderer — consistent with a full `agent-browser` daemon-managed session that was never torn down
- The owning hermes gateway process itself (`/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python -m hermes_cli.main gateway run`) was confirmed alive and running the entire time (single PID since Jul 15, no restarts)
- Load average on the 4-core host reached 8.72 as a direct result
- Killing all 117 processes (`pkill -9 -f "usr/lib/chromium"`) was safe — did not affect the running gateway process, and load average began dropping immediately

## Suspected root cause

Reading `_reap_orphaned_browser_sessions()` (tools/browser_tool.py, ~line 1311):

```python
if os.path.isfile(owner_pid_file):
    try:
        owner_pid = int(Path(owner_pid_file).read_text(...).strip())
        owner_alive = _pid_exists(owner_pid)
    except (ValueError, OSError):
        owner_alive = None

if owner_alive is True:
    # Owner is alive — this session belongs to a live hermes process.
    continue
```

The `owner_pid` file appears to record the **hermes gateway process PID**, not a per-session/per-daemon identifier. On a long-running gateway (the normal/intended operating mode — it's supposed to stay up), `owner_pid` is *always* alive, so `owner_alive is True` short-circuits the reaper for every single daemon that process has ever spawned — the reap loop `continue`s before ever reaching the per-session `_active_sessions` tracking fallback (which is only consulted when `owner_alive is None`, i.e. no owner_pid file at all).

In other words: the ownership check is process-granularity, but it needs to be session/daemon-granularity. A daemon whose *specific* browser session has ended (or crashed) but whose *parent hermes process* is still running (normal operation) is never reaped, because "owner is alive" is treated as sufden for "leave this daemon alone" regardless of whether that daemon still corresponds to a live, tracked session.

This would explain why orphans only accumulate on long-lived gateway processes and never get cleaned up — the reaper effectively only fires for daemons whose *entire hermes process* died (crash/SIGKILL/restart), which is a much rarer case than a browser session/daemon dying independently while the gateway keeps running.

## Suggested fix direction

The reap loop's fallback path (checking `_active_sessions` in the current process) should probably run *unconditionally* when `owner_alive is True` too — not just when `owner_alive is None`. I.e.: if the owner process is this same live process, check whether the session is still tracked in `_active_sessions`; if it isn't (session ended/errored but daemon wasn't torn down), still reap it. Only skip reaping when the owner is a *different, live* hermes process (cross-process safety, which is the scenario `owner_pid` was designed for).

Alternatively/additionally: track owner at daemon-launch granularity (e.g. a monotonic per-session token) rather than raw process PID, so "is the specific session still valid" and "is the owning process still alive" are answered independently.

## Workaround in place

Deployed a blunt daily watchdog (`orphaned-chromium-watchdog.sh`) via cron that kills any `chromium` process older than a configurable threshold (default 6h) regardless of the reaper's internal state, as a safety net. This works but doesn't address the underlying gap — happy to share the script if useful as a reference for a test case, but it's not a substitute for fixing the reaper logic.

## Impact

On resource-constrained hosts (4-core LXC container in this case), this leak drove sustained load average to 8.72, and each orphaned session held ~100-170MB RSS per Chromium sub-process (~1GB+ per orphaned session, ~10GB+ total across 13 sessions) — a real and growing resource leak on any long-running gateway deployment that uses the browser tool regularly.

items.body:
## Summary

After switching the model via the desktop app's model picker, `config.yaml`'s `custom_providers` model entries can get corrupted: string model names are serialized as **per-character mappings** instead of plain strings.

## Example (observed on v0.19.1, Windows 10)

```yaml
custom_providers:
  - name: fennoai-copy
    base_url: https://api.asxs.top/v1
    models:
      gpt-5.5:
        '0': g
        '1': p
        '2': t
        '3': '-'
        '4': '5'
        '5': .
        '6': '6'
        '7': '-'
        '8': l
        '9': u
        '10': n
        '11': a
        name: gpt-5.5
```

The mapping `{'0':'g','1':'p',...}` decodes to the string `gpt-5.6-luna` — i.e. a model-name string that existed in the config at some point got written out as a character-index dict. Both `fennoai` and `fennoai-copy` providers were affected; in one entry the corruption was cross-contaminated between two model entries (`gpt-5.6-sol`'s mapping decodes to `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.5`'s mapping decodes to `gpt-5.6-luna`).

## Impact

- Currently **harmless** in practice: Hermes resolves models by the YAML **key** (`gpt-5.5`), and the character mappings are ignored. Model calls work (76 successful calls observed).
- It is structurally broken config, and anything that reads the `name`/mapping fields (e.g. a future version, or tooling that round-trips the config) can misbehave. It also makes the config very hard to read.

## Likely source

The desktop model picker's config write path serializing a string value as a dict (per-character index → char). This matches a write that happens when the user switches models in the desktop app's input-bar model selector.

## Suggested fix

- In the desktop config-write path, ensure model-name strings are written as YAML strings, never expanded into a character mapping.
- Optionally: on config load, detect and repair/ignore non-string dict shapes under `models.*` (warn + treat the key as the model name).

items.title: Updater: 'close all Hermes processes' dead-end + stale update lock — needs auto-remediation or doctor on failure

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Summary

The Hermes updater's "close all Hermes processes" requirement is a dead end in practice: even with every Hermes process closed (only the updater itself left running), the update can still refuse and demand that all Hermes processes be closed — and in the worst case the updater process itself ends up terminated, leaving the user stuck with a broken update and no way forward.

## Reproduction / experience (Windows 10, v0.19.0 → v0.19.1 era)

1. Launch an update while the desktop app is running.
2. The updater errors: *"Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again."*
3. User closes the desktop app and every Hermes-related process (verified: only the updater process remains).
4. The updater still reports the same "another update is already running / Hermes is still running" error — a leftover updater PID from an earlier attempt (PID that no longer exists) keeps the update locked.
5. The user eventually kills the updater process too, and there is no automated help — no `doctor`-style diagnostics, no auto-remediation.

Separately, the "another update is already running (PID X)" guard can hold a stale PID: the original update process died, but the lock isn't cleared, so every retry fails instantly for hours until a reboot.

## Suggested improvements (either would fix the experience)

1. **Auto-terminate blockers**: when an update starts, have the updater (or a launcher with sufficient privileges) automatically close Hermes desktop/gateway processes itself, instead of demanding the user do it manually — or at minimum, detect that the blocking processes are gone/stale and proceed.
2. **Stale-lock recovery**: if the recorded "already running" PID no longer exists, treat the lock as stale and take it over instead of erroring forever.
3. **Failure path → diagnostics**: when an update/install fails, offer an automatic `hermes doctor`-style run that explains why (which process is blocking, stale PID, disk space, network to GitHub, etc.) and suggests the concrete fix.

## Environment

- Hermes v0.19.0 → v0.19.1 updater (Windows 10, desktop install)
- Stale-updater lock persisted across retries for hours; only a reboot cleared it

items.title: Expose authenticated channel-to-session discovery for dashboard PTY sidecars
items.body:
## Problem

The dashboard PTY sidecar event channel can be consumed by authenticated clients, but those clients cannot discover which durable Hermes session is currently active on that channel.

At `003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd`:

- `/api/pty?channel=...` allocates a per-channel active-session file and injects it as `HERMES_TUI_ACTIVE_SESSION_FILE`.
- The TUI updates that file on create/resume/switch, and `/api/pty` uses it to resume the channel after reconnect.
- `/api/events?channel=...` streams dispatcher frames for the same channel, but does not provide an initial binding record or an authenticated query for the channel's current durable `session_id`.

Relevant source:

- [`hermes_cli/web_server.py` channel active-session tracking](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L14813-L14841)
- [`/api/pty` active-session fallback](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L15474-L15505)
- [`/api/events` channel subscription](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/003af7f85ce2ebe24b38556d735a0d7678a4a8dd/hermes_cli/web_server.py#L15668-L15709)

Parsing PTY output is not a safe substitute, and guessing from the session database is ambiguous when several profiles or sessions are active.

## Requested contract

Expose the current channel binding through either:

1. an authenticated, read-only endpoint keyed by channel; or
2. a structured control frame delivered first on `/api/events` subscription and whenever the binding changes.

A minimal response/event could contain:

- channel identifier;
- durable `session_id`;
- profile identity when the channel is profile-scoped;
- a monotonic binding generation or revision;
- binding state such as `bound`, `switching`, or `cleared`.

No prompt, message, reasoning, tool content, PTY bytes, paths, credentials, or environment values are needed.

## Lifecycle expectations

- Publish/update the binding after create, resume, and session switch.
- A newly subscribed event client receives the current binding before later session-scoped events, or receives a generation that lets it reject stale frames.
- `fresh=1`, PTY child exit, registry eviction, and channel teardown clear or replace the binding truthfully.
- Authentication and host/origin checks are at least as strict as `/api/pty` and `/api/events`.
- Concurrent reconnects cannot expose an older binding as current after a newer switch.

## Why this helps

This lets external dashboard/desktop consumers correlate sidecar lifecycle events with the same durable session used by Hermes without scraping terminal output or inventing a parallel session authority.

items.title: [Bug]: Local custom-provider MCP tool result (unfiltered list_entities) exceeds context, compression exhausts 3 attempts — inconsistent agent_close vs explicit error

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Bug Description

On a local custom-provider setup (vLLM, `-t metamcp` toolset), a single MCP tool call
(`homeassistant__list_entities`, called with no query filter) returns an oversized JSON
result (the model's own reasoning reported "over 900,000 characters... too much to work
with directly"). Auto-compression exhausts its 3 attempts trying to make room, and the turn
fails — but with two *different* observed failure modes for what looks like the same
underlying condition:

1. Sometimes an explicit error: `Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.`
2. Sometimes a **silent** `end_reason: agent_close` with no error message at all, mid-reasoning,
   right before the model would have made the next (data-retrieval) tool call.

This looks related to #61932 (protected recent tail defeats compression) and #62605
(token-estimate gap), but reproduced on a **local custom OpenAI-compatible provider** (not
Desktop/openai-codex), with the added inconsistent-failure-mode wrinkle.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), upstream `eb527605`
- Provider: custom, OpenAI-compatible, local vLLM 0.26.0 serving a Qwen3.5-MoE model
  (compressed-tensors quant), `--max-model-len 131072`
- Hermes config `context_length` for this model: `262144` — note: **larger** than the
  server's actual `--max-model-len 131072`. Possible contributing mismatch, not isolated as
  root cause.
- Compression config: `threshold: 0.5, target_ratio: 0.2, protect_last_n: 20, protect_first_n: 3`
- Invocation: `hermes -z "<prompt>" -t metamcp --yolo --cli`

## Reproduction

1. `hermes -z "<question requiring miner energy consumption>" -t metamcp --yolo --cli`
2. Model calls `homeassistant__list_entities` with no arguments → full entity list returned
   (model's own reasoning: "over 900,000 characters... too much to work with directly")
3. Turn fails.

Reproduced 3x across a 50+ minute window (once right after container start, once again
~47 min later) with the identical prompt — ruling out a simple cold-start/warm-up
explanation.

**Run 1** (`tool_call_count: 2`, `end_reason: agent_close`): turn stopped mid-reasoning
after 2 tool calls (`list_entities`, `search_entities`), right before the planned 3rd call
(`get_statistics`). No error surfaced to the CLI at all — just silence, 37s wall time.

**Run 2** (immediate retry, identical prompt): explicit
`Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.` after 2m8s.

## Why this looks related but distinct

- Same failure text/mechanism as #61932 (`protect_last_n`-style: the oversized tool-result
  message is recent, so it sits in the protected tail and can't be shrunk) — but #61932 was
  reported+closed for Desktop/openai-codex; this reproduces on the bare local
  custom-provider CLI oneshot (`-z`) path.
- Possibly related to #62605 (token-estimate gap): this session's recorded
  `input_tokens: 69,545` for the failed turn seems inconsistent with the model's own claim
  that the raw tool result alone was ~900,000 characters (roughly 200-300K tokens on its
  own) — Hermes' size accounting for this tool result may be significantly off, though I
  haven't traced `estimate_request_tokens_rough` myself to confirm.
- New wrinkle not covered by either: **two different failure modes for the same trigger**
  -- sometimes a clean error, sometimes a completely silent `agent_close`. The silent case is
  worse for debuggability -- nothing at all reaches the end user, not even a truncated
  response.

## Suggested angle (observation, not a fix)

#43059 fixed the PDF-specific instance of "one oversized tool result kills the turn" by
refusing to read the file as text at all. A more general fix might cap/summarize individual
MCP tool results above some size threshold *before* they enter the protected tail, since
per #61932 compression can't touch protected-tail content anyway. Happy to share a sanitized
session export if useful.

items.title: Feature Request: RTL (Right-to-Left) Language Support

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Problem

All text in Hermes Agent is LTR. For RTL languages (Persian, Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu), this causes:

- Chat messages force RTL text into wrong alignment
- Mixed Persian/English content breaks bidirectional rendering
- Markdown tables, lists, and blockquotes display incorrectly
- Persian/Arabic filenames in file browser are misaligned

### Proposed Solution

1. **Per-message direction** — Auto-detect text direction from content, or let users set it.
2. **Markdown-aware bidirectionality** — RTL flow for prose, always LTR for code blocks/paths.
3. **UI mirroring** — Sidebar, buttons, and panels mirror when RTL is active.
4. **Config option** — `direction: auto | rtl | ltr` in settings.

### Why

RTL is essential, not cosmetic. Persian/Arabic speakers cannot comfortably use the app without it. Chromium/Electron already has CSS `direction` + `unicode-bidi` — implementation is straightforward.

### Environment

- **OS:** Windows 10/11
- **App:** Hermes Agent Desktop

items.body:
## Summary

The desktop app's **Settings → Custom Endpoints** panel is **not profile-scoped**: it always reads and writes the *primary* backend's config, regardless of which profile is active. This makes the panel show endpoints from the wrong profile ("already exists" for an endpoint that is not in the active profile) and silently save edits to the wrong profile's `config.yaml`.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30) · upstream 003af7f8 (installed from git, macOS arm64)
- Desktop app (Hermes.app), two profiles: `default` + `mac-mini`
- Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LiteLLM at `http://172.17.9.1:4000/v1`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run the desktop app with the **default** profile active. Add a custom endpoint via **Settings → Providers → Custom Endpoints** (base URL, API key, model). It is saved to the default profile's `config.yaml` under `providers.<id>` and `model.provider` points at it.
2. Switch the desktop app to a **second profile** (e.g. `mac-mini`). Open **Settings → Models**: the provider dropdown is correctly profile-scoped and does **not** show the custom endpoint (good).
3. Open **Settings → Providers → Custom Endpoints** in the same second profile: the panel *does* show the endpoint from the **default** profile ("LiteLLM" already exists), even though the active profile's config has no such entry.

## Expected behavior

The Custom Endpoints panel must be scoped to the **active profile**, matching Settings → Models. In the active profile, it should show only that profile's endpoints; saving/validating/activating/deleting must target the active profile's `config.yaml` (and its `.env` for the key).

## Actual behavior

- The panel shows the **primary** profile's endpoints regardless of the active profile (misleading "already exists" / "configured" state).
- Saving through the panel writes to the **primary** profile's config even when the user believes they are configuring the active profile.

## Root cause

In `apps/desktop/src/hermes.ts`, the five custom-endpoint API helpers do **not** spread `profileScoped()`, unlike neighboring helpers and unlike the model-options helper used by Settings → Models:

- `getCustomEndpoints()` — line 796
- `saveCustomEndpoint()` — line 802
- `validateCustomEndpoint()` — line 810
- `activateCustomEndpoint()` — line 818
- `deleteCustomEndpoint()` — line 825

For contrast, `deleteEnvVar()` / `revealEnvVar()` (lines 832–848) and `getGlobalModelOptions()` (line 1456) all spread `...profileScoped()`, so they correctly target the active profile's backend. Because `request.profile` is what Electron main uses to route the call to the right backend process (each pooled backend has its own `HERMES_HOME`), the missing spread means the custom-endpoints calls always land on the primary backend.

The backend side (`hermes_cli/web_server.py`, `/api/providers/custom-endpoints*`, lines 7226–7336) already supports the `profile` param for other endpoints; the custom-endpoints routes just never receive it.

## Impact

Multi-profile desktop users get a panel that lies about configuration state and writes to the wrong profile. In our case this manifested as: endpoint registered on the default profile, invisible in Settings → Models on the second profile, while the Custom Endpoints panel claimed it "already exists" — leading to confusion about which profile was configured. Only the CLI path (`hermes config set` / `hermes model`) reliably targets the active profile.

## Suggested fix

Add `...profileScoped()` to the five helpers in `apps/desktop/src/hermes.ts` (lines 796–830), consistent with `getGlobalModelOptions()` and the env helpers. Optionally, verify the backend routes honor the `profile` param the same way other `/api/*` routes do.

---

*Filed on behalf of a user by an AI assistant (Hermes Agent) at the user's explicit direction, after we diagnosed the issue together on a local multi-profile setup. The user encountered the behavior described above and asked that it be reported.*

items.body:
## Summary

Recent directives sent through a Buzz ACP-connected Hermes instance were not
retrievable from another Hermes gateway session via `session_search`.

This breaks cross-platform continuity: I sent two messages in Buzz at
approximately 1:48 PM local time, then asked the same Hermes installation from
Telegram to identify them. It could not find them and incorrectly concluded
they might not have arrived.

## Expected behavior

Messages that have been received and processed by `hermes acp` should be stored
and indexed so that `session_search` can retrieve them from another Hermes
session/transport.

For example, a user should be able to send a task in Buzz, then ask from
Telegram: “What were my last two Buzz directives?” and receive a grounded
answer from the stored ACP conversation history.

If cross-transport search is intentionally unsupported, the response should
make that boundary explicit rather than silently returning no relevant results.

## Actual behavior

From a Telegram gateway session, `session_search` did not find the recent Buzz
directives.

The host logs nevertheless show that the Buzz ACP harness was running and
passing prompts into Hermes:

text
Aug 01 19:27:43 ... acp_adapter.server: Prompt on session <redacted>
Aug 01 19:27:43 ... agent.turn_context: conversation turn:
  model=gemma4:12b provider=custom platform=acp history=18

Aug 01 19:35:30 ... acp_adapter.server: Prompt on session <redacted>
Aug 01 19:35:30 ... agent.turn_context: conversation turn:
  model=gemma4:12b provider=custom platform=acp history=26


So this does not appear to be a Unix filesystem permission issue or a missing
ACP process. The ACP subprocess and the normal Hermes gateway run as the same
Unix user.

## Why this matters

A user can legitimately continue work from a different connected platform.
When the history lookup fails, Hermes may claim a task was never sent or cannot
determine whether it arrived, even when the ACP service did receive it.

This is particularly problematic for configuration and operational requests
that are issued in one channel and followed up from another.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `v0.19.1 (2026.7.30)`
- Hermes checkout revision: `470cf66b0`
- Python: `3.11.15`
- OpenAI SDK: `2.24.0`
- Transport where directives were sent: Buzz via ACP
- Follow-up transport: Telegram gateway
- Buzz source revision: `3e48f1b`
- ACP process: `buzz-acp` launching `hermes acp`
- Host OS: Linux
- Date observed: 2026-08-01

## Related but possibly separate observation

The Buzz ACP session used `gemma4:12b` and repeatedly logged:

text
Response truncated (finish_reason='length') - model hit max output tokens


This occurred several times during the ACP session. It may be a separate
failure-recovery issue, but the primary issue here is that the recent ACP
messages could not be found by `session_search` from another gateway session.

## Security / redaction

Session IDs, credentials, private keys, API keys, and message contents have
been omitted from this report. I can provide additional redacted diagnostics if
maintainers need them.

text of original prompts sent in Buzz
@Herman Could you check if poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free is in our model list for Openrouter , if not please add it
@Herman Report back with any issues and when complete

I ran `hermes update` earlier on the same day this occurred. At the time of
collection, the local checkout was `470cf66b0`; additional commits had landed
upstream afterward, so this is not simply an outdated-install report.

Report created with Hermes assistance
